newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Don't let computers control your kids, Euro-MP warns.
newsitem.headline: Don't let computers control your kids, Euro-MP warns.

text.p: Children of the future may carry information in their trainers instead of their heads and wear "smarty pants" which regulate their classroom temperature, Euro-MP Eluned Morgan predicted on Wednesday.
"Futuristic technologies (are) the stuff of science fact not of science fiction," the British Socialist told a press conference to launch her report on education, culture and the information society.
Morgan said developments in computer technology and the Internet offered marvellous opportunities for children and adults to have almost instant access to information on every subject under the sun.

But she warned that unless national governments and the European Union addressed a whole series of problems soon, computers could end up controlling people and the gulf between the technology haves and have nots would split society down the middle.
"We need to use technology so it serves education and culture and not have our education and technology determined by the new technology," Morgan said.
The potential is enormous, Morgan's report says.

A computer linked directly to the brain could help disabled children learn, while interactive multi-media "edutainment" programmes could help prevent pupils failing at school by simultaneously teaching and amusing them.
Computer learning programmes could better enable children to progress at their own pace, both in and out of school and allow adults to retrain without giving up work.

New technology could allow schoolchildren in Morgan's constituency of West Wales to see and hear about works of art in the Paris Louvre and do a joint weather project with pupils in Rimini and Reykjavik without leaving the room.

There are even prototypes of computer-bearing trainers, into which children can download whole books and carry their homework, and "wearable" memory computers which record everything a person sees and hears in their lifetime.
But there are pitfalls, Morgan warned.
Not every parent can afford new smart shoes, especially when their offspring outgrow them every two months or persist in wearing them to play football on the way home.
And what if the kids use their wearable computers to cheat in exams or remind their parents of a promise they would rather forget?
What if they become so reliant on computers that they never actually learn how to add up or talk to other people?
How can society avoid a surge in inequality between a technological computer-literate elite and the increasingly marginalised rest?
Morgan said she wanted the European Commission to work with national governments, schools, software companies and the private sector to start tackling these problems now.

For example, the Commission could encourage public-private partnerships, such as getting businesses and local authorities to provide schools and libraries with Internet-linked computers, and then use the equipment to train their own staff during the evening.

As well as increasing public access to on-line educational material, Morgan wants the Commission and the member states to fund a free public "millennium archive" containing national cultural collections in digital form.

She criticised Britain's national art gallery for selling its digital rights to the American software giant Microsoft, obliging the British public to pay a foreign firm to access their own cultural heritage.
The Euro-MP said she was also very concerned that both pupils, teachers and parents should learn not just to access information on the Internet but also to analyse and interpret it intelligently.
